name: Caodaism
info: Caodaism is a Vietnamese monotheistic syncretic religion, founded in Saigon in 1925 and officially established at Tây Ninh in 1926, that joins Confucian ethics, Taoist practice, Buddhist ideas of karma and rebirth and a hierarchical organisation from Catholicism.

facts.origin: Saigon, Southern Vietnam, in 1925, as a Spiritualist club; officially established in the city of Tây Ninh in 1926.
facts.founder: Cao Quỳnh Cư, Cao Hoài Sang, Lê Văn Trung and Phạm Công Tắc, clerks in the colonial government who founded the Spiritualist club in 1925; Ngô Văn Chiêu, revered as the first disciple of the Đức Cao Đài, signed the declaration of founding on 7 October 1926.
facts.scriptures: Several sets of scriptures; those of the Tây Ninh Holy See include Kinh Thiên Đạo Và Thế Đạo (Prayers of the Heavenly and the Earthly Way), Pháp Chánh Truyền (the Religious Constitution), Tân Luật (the Canonical Codes) and Con Đường Thiêng Liêng Hằng Sống (Divine Path to Eternal Life).
facts.followers: Estimates vary: government figures give 4.4 million affiliated to the Tây Ninh Holy See and up to 6 million with other branches; the United Nations estimated about 2.5 million in Vietnam in January 2015; tens of thousands live abroad, mainly in North America, Cambodia, Europe and Australia.

t: Caodaists worship one God, Cao Đài, and hold that all religions come from the same source; they believe that God has revealed his will in three eras and that the third and final revelation is given through the Cao Đài faith.
The religion began in 1925 in Saigon with a group of colonial clerks who held séances, and was officially established at Tây Ninh in 1926; by 1940 it had gathered over a million members.
Its church is organised in a hierarchy with a Pope, Cardinals, Bishops and Priests, and its clergy wear yellow, azure or red for the Buddhist, Taoist and Confucianist branches.
dyk: Caodaists hold that Victor Hugo, Sun Yat-sen and Trạng Trình, the Vietnamese Nostradamus, are the three main prophets of the Cao Đài pantheon, as a plaque at the entrance of the Tây Ninh Temple shows.

sections.origins:
Caodaism, officially Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ, the “Great Way of the Third Era of Redemption”, is a Vietnamese monotheistic syncretic religion. It combines ethical precepts from Confucianism, practices from Taoism, theories of karma and rebirth from Buddhism and a hierarchical organisation from Catholicism. It was founded in 1925 in Saigon as a Spiritualist club named AĂÂ by Cao Quỳnh Cư, Cao Hoài Sang, Lê Văn Trung and Phạm Công Tắc, a group of clerks working in the colonial government, to practise mediumship and ouija sessions. They were avid readers of the medium writings of Allan Kardec, Victor Hugo and Flammarion.

During a séance in 1926 the group believed they had received a revelation predicting a future universal religion based on spiritist doctrines. The message gave the member Ngô Văn Chiêu a religious mission in life, which led to his signing of the “Declaration of the Founding of the Cao Đài Religion” on 7 October 1926. The religion was officially established in the city of Tây Ninh in Southern Vietnam in 1926 and soon grew into a religious movement.

Ngô Văn Chiêu, revered in Caodaism as the first disciple of the Đức Cao Đài, had never intended it to become a mass organisation. He disagreed with proselytisation and wished to keep the practice esoteric. He declined the appointment as Pope and left the movement, eventually establishing an independent, esoteric branch known as Chiếu Minh, headquartered in Vĩnh Long, which admits only a limited number of committed adepts. Lê Văn Trung took the more exoteric approach and became the acting Pope.
sections.beliefs:
Caodaists worship one God, called Cao Đài, also known as the Supreme Being, Creator and Ngọc Hoàng. The full title, Cao Đài Tiên Ông Đại Bồ Tát Ma Ha Tát, combines three religions: Cao Đài, “High Tower” or “High Palace”, stands for Confucianism, Tiên Ông, the highest rank in Taoism, for Taoism, and Đại Bồ Tát Ma Ha Tát, “Great Bodhisattva, the Great Being”, for Mahayana Buddhism. Caodaists hold that God permeates all things and that part of his spirit is within every person and creature. They hold that all religions derive from the same source and that God has many names.

Caodaists adopt the Chinese idea of âm (yin) and dương (yang). There are two main Gods: Cao Đài, the yang force and the common Father of all beings, and Diêu Trì Kim Mẫu or Đức Phật Mẫu, the Holy Buddha Mother, the yin force, who gives visible forms, consciousness and emotions to all life. Believers hold that heaven and hell are the main destinations of souls after death and that souls must cultivate virtue to escape the cycle of birth and death, true liberation coming when a soul rejoins God the Father in heaven.

Monthly rituals take place at midnight on the 1st and 15th days of the lunar month, with an annual ceremony for God the Father, the Holy Mother, the founders of the world’s major religions and the founders of Caodaism. The most important festival is the Holy Banquet for the Great Mother and the Nine Goddesses, held at Tây Ninh on the 15th of the eighth lunar month. Believers practise prayer, veneration of ancestors, nonviolence and vegetarianism.
sections.texts:
There are various Caodaist scriptures. Those of the Tây Ninh Holy See include Kinh Thiên Đạo Và Thế Đạo (“Prayers of the Heavenly and the Earthly Way”), Pháp Chánh Truyền (“the Religious Constitution of Cao Đài Religion”), Tân Luật (“The Canonical Codes”) and Con Đường Thiêng Liêng Hằng Sống (“Divine Path to Eternal Life”). The Religious Constitution was delivered to the religion as a series of divine messages. It guides the religion’s organisation, setting out the authority, responsibility, limits and vestments of each rank.

The Canonical Codes set out the rules and boundaries for different aspects of the religion, from a believer to the Pope, from education to marriage. Its ten sections cover the hierarchy of religious dignitaries, the initiation and ranks of believers, the establishment of a parish, the five interdictions, the four commandments, education, sanctions, the promulgation of laws and regulations, secular rules and the house of meditation.

Caodaists believe that Cao Đài has communed with humankind since the beginning of time, and that history is divided into three eras of revelation. In the first two, Dipankara Buddha, Fu Xi, Gautama Buddha, Laozi, Confucius and Jesus received the will of the Highest Power and founded their religions, which Caodaists believe were corrupted and applied only to certain peoples and ages. The third and final revelation is disclosed through the teachings of the Cao Đài faith.
sections.spread:
The religion was founded in Saigon in 1925 and officially established at Tây Ninh in 1926, and it soon grew into a religious movement. During the 1930s its leader criticised yet maintained good ties with the French colonial regime, a stance that was controversial and contrasted with the liturgy of dozens of “dissident” branches that followed a more Taoist model. By 1940 it had gathered over a million members, converting a fifth to a quarter of the population of Cochinchina.

The period between 1934 and 1975 saw both the robust development of the religion and its separation into different independent sects, sometimes as many as thirty. These generally divide along geographic lines. The largest is based in Tây Ninh Province, where the religion was founded and where its seat of authority is located. Sects that broke away from the Tây Ninh Holy See include Cầu Kho, Bến Tre, Minh Chơn Lý, Minh Chơn Đạo, Tiên Thiên and Hội Thánh Truyền Giáo Trung Việt, and Ngô Văn Chiêu founded Chiếu Minh when he left the original church structure.

In the 1940s the leaders were jailed in Madagascar, and after 1975 the religion was banned in Vietnam. Today, besides its followers in Vietnam, tens of thousands, primarily ethnic Vietnamese, live in North America, Cambodia, Europe and Australia as part of the Cao Đài diaspora.
sections.community:
The organisation of the Caodaist church resembles that of a state and has similarities with that of the Catholic Church. Besides the Pope, the hierarchy has Cardinals, Bishops, Priests and further ranks. The religion is governed by two powers, the spiritual and the earthly. The spiritual power is the heavenly council, made up of Divine Beings and directed by God the Father. The earthly power is divided into an Executive Body headed by the Pope, which administers the religion and its missionary activities, and a Legislative Body headed by the Hộ Pháp, which oversees legislation, jurisdiction and communication with the Divine Beings. The Giáo Tông, or Pope, is the head of the Executive Body. The first and only officially ordained Pope of the Tây Ninh Holy See was Lê Văn Trung (1876–1934), and after his death the position was left permanently vacant.

Male dignitaries of the Executive Body wear yellow for the Buddhist branch, azure for the Taoist branch and red for the Confucianist branch. Any local area with more than 500 believers may establish a parish with a temple, with the Pope’s permission, and believers must meet at the temple on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, unless they have a reasonable excuse.

Caodaism stresses equality of men and women in society. In the spiritual domain, however, ordained women may not attain the two highest positions, the Legislative Cardinal and the Pope; the church claims this is ordered by the Highest Lord, who declared that Yin cannot dominate Yang spiritually or chaos ensues.
sections.legacy:
During the First and Second Indochina Wars members of Cao Đài, with those of several other Vietnamese sects such as Hòa Hảo, were active in political and military struggles against both the French colonial forces and the South Vietnamese Prime Minister Ngô Đình Diệm, who later became president. From 1941 to 1946 Phạm Công Tắc and other leaders were arrested and jailed in French penal colonies in Madagascar. Their criticism of the communist forces until 1975 was a factor in the repression that followed the fall of Saigon in April 1975, when the incoming communist government banned the practice of Caodaism. In 1997 it was granted legal recognition and unrestricted practice once again.

Estimates of the number of Caodaists in Vietnam vary. Government figures give 4.4 million affiliated to the Tây Ninh Holy See and up to 6 million with other branches, while the United Nations estimated about 2.5 million in January 2015. As of July 2014 central and provincial authorities had granted legal recognition to 11 Cao Đài sects.

The Tây Ninh Executive Council received official government recognition in 1997. Independent Caodaist groups allege that government interference has undermined the independence of the Tây Ninh group and that it no longer faithfully upholds Cao Đài’s principles and traditions. The Tây Ninh Holy See, with the Great Divine Temple at its heart, is the major centre of Caodaist pilgrimage and one of Vietnam’s major tourist attractions.

summary: Caodaism is a Vietnamese monotheistic religion founded in Saigon in 1925 and established at Tây Ninh in 1926, drawing on Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism and Catholic organisation. Its followers worship God as Cao Đài and hold all religions to share one source. It was banned after 1975 and recognised again in 1997.
references: Janet Alison Hoskins, The Divine Eye and the Diaspora: Vietnamese syncretism becomes transpacific Caodaism (University of Hawaii Press, 2015)
Victor L. Oliver, Caodai Spiritism: A Study of Religion in Vietnamese Society (BRILL, 1976)
Jayne Werner, Peasant Politics and Religious Sectarianism: Peasant and Priest in the Cao Dai in Vietnam (Yale University Southeast Asian Studies, 1981)
notes: Start 1925: the club AĂÂ founded in Saigon; the article also says the religion was officially established at Tây Ninh in 1926 (declaration signed 7 October 1926). The first event keeps 1925 and the second 1926.

Sources conflict slightly: the article lists the five founders of religions in the spiritual council as including Jiang Ziya (Geniism), while the revelation section names Dipankara, Fu Xi, Gautama, Laozi, Confucius and Jesus; the profile uses only the revelation list in the texts section.
The article says a fifth to a fourth of Cochinchina’s population; written as ‘a fifth to a quarter’. The ‘Holy Banquet’ is also spelled Cao Dai / Caodaiists in places.
Left out: the detail of the Divine Eye, banner and emblem, the symbols and the long list of Hiệp Thiên Đài offices.

Faith map: the article gives no dates for the diaspora, so those areas start with the 2015 UN estimate (1 level); Chiếu Minh’s founding date is not stated, so it has no mark. Only one route (the leaders to Madagascar, 1941) is supported by the article. Coordinates of Saigon, Tây Ninh, Madagascar, Cochinchina, Cambodia, North America, Europe and Australia are general geography.
Followers: figures are the article’s; the 2.5 million UN figure is as of January 2015.
